u.src: The Algebra of Brackets
en: The Algebra of Brackets

p.src:
The bracket can now be used as a calculus of its own. Its rules follow from ordinary differentiation: $\begin{aligned}
  \{A,B\}&=-\{B,A\}, \\
  \{A+B,C\}&=\{A,C\}+\{B,C\}, \\
  \{\lambda A,B\}&=\lambda\{A,B\},
    \quad \lambda\ \text{constant}, \\
  \{AB,C\}&=A\{B,C\}+\{A,C\}B. \end{aligned}$ These four lines express antisymmetry, additivity, linearity under multiplication by a constant, and the Leibniz rule, respectively. Classical phase-space functions multiply commutatively, so the placement of the ordinary factors $A$ and $B$ in the last line is immaterial. That will no longer be true for operators in quantum mechanics. Antisymmetry also implies $\{A,A\}=0.$

p.src:
For canonical coordinates the elementary brackets are $\boxed{
  \{q_i,q_j\}=0,\qquad
  \{p_i,p_j\}=0,\qquad
  \{q_i,p_j\}=\delta_{ij}.}$ Any function only of the $q_i$ has zero bracket with any other function only of the $q_i$; the analogous statement holds for functions only of the $p_i$. A nonzero bracket requires a canonical coordinate to meet its conjugate momentum. The Kronecker delta in Eq.  records that only matching indices meet.

p.src:
Consider $H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac{kq^2}{2}.$ We now deliberately use only the bracket rules and Eq. . First, $\begin{aligned}
  \dot q
  &=\{q,H\}\\
  &=\frac{1}{2m}\{q,p^2\}\\
  &=\frac{1}{2m}\left(p\{q,p\}+\{q,p\}p\right)\\
  &=\frac{p}{m}.
  \end{aligned}$ The potential term disappears because $\{q,q^2\}=0$. Similarly, $\begin{aligned}
  \dot p
  &=\{p,H\}\\
  &=\frac{k}{2}\{p,q^2\}\\
  &=\frac{k}{2}\left(q\{p,q\}+\{p,q\}q\right)\\
  &=-kq.
  \end{aligned}$ The minus sign is precisely the antisymmetry $\{p,q\}=-\{q,p\}=-1$. Combining the two first-order equations gives $m\ddot q=-kq.$

p.src: Recall the infinitesimal form of Noether’s construction used earlier in the course. If a continuous symmetry changes the coordinates by $\delta q_i=\epsilon F_i(q),$ then, in the setting considered here, its conserved quantity is $G=\sum_i p_iF_i(q).$ The overall factor $\epsilon$ may be omitted: multiplying a conserved quantity by a fixed number does not change the conservation law.

p.src:
Take one particle and rotate it infinitesimally about the $z$-axis. With the orientation used in the lecture, $\delta x=-\epsilon y,\qquad
  \delta y=\epsilon x,\qquad
  \delta z=0.$ Equation  gives $L_z=-p_xy+p_yx=xp_y-yp_x.$ Cycling $x$, $y$, and $z$, $\boxed{\begin{aligned}
    L_x&=yp_z-zp_y,\\
    L_y&=zp_x-xp_z,\\
    L_z&=xp_y-yp_x.
  \end{aligned}}$ These are the components of $\boldsymbol L=\boldsymbol r\times\boldsymbol p.$

If only rotations around one axis remain a symmetry, only the component along that axis is guaranteed to be conserved.

p.src:
The next calculation lets us stop dragging the particle coordinates through every rotational problem. Begin with $L_x=yp_z-zp_y,\qquad
  L_z=xp_y-yp_x.$ In $\{L_x,L_z\}$, most cross terms vanish because their indices do not form canonical pairs. The surviving contractions give $\begin{aligned}
  \{L_x,L_z\}
  &=\{yp_z-zp_y,xp_y-yp_x\}\\
  &=xp_z-zp_x\\
  &=-L_y.
  \end{aligned}$ Reversing the order removes the minus sign. Cycling the coordinates produces $\boxed{\begin{aligned}
    \{L_x,L_y\}&=L_z,\\
    \{L_y,L_z\}&=L_x,\\
    \{L_z,L_x\}&=L_y.
  \end{aligned}}$ In index notation, $\{L_i,L_j\}=\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k.$

p.src: A Fast Gyroscope

u.src: A Fast Gyroscope
en: A Fast Gyroscope

p.src:
As an application, consider a gyroscope: a rapidly spinning flywheel whose center is a fixed distance $R$ from a pivot. Let $\boldsymbol r$ point from the pivot to the wheel center. The flywheel spins so rapidly about its axle that its dominant angular momentum remains aligned with that direction. In the approximation used in the lecture, $\boldsymbol L=\ell\,\boldsymbol r,
  \qquad
  L_z=\ell z,$ where $\ell=L/R$ is treated as constant. Smaller angular momenta associated with nutation or motion of the axle are neglected at first.

p.src:
Take the vertical coordinate $z$ positive upward and put the pivot at the origin. The gravitational potential energy of the wheel center is $V=Mgz.$ Since $L_z=\ell z$, $V=cL_z,
  \qquad
  c=\frac{Mg}{\ell}=\frac{MgR}{L}.$ Here $c>0$ when $\boldsymbol L$ is chosen parallel to $\boldsymbol r$. If the flywheel spins in the opposite sense, the signed relation between $\boldsymbol L$ and $\boldsymbol r$ reverses and so does the corresponding signed precession frequency.

p.src:
The full reduced Hamiltonian is $H=
  \frac{1}{2I}\left(L_x^2+L_y^2+L_z^2\right)+cL_z.$ We have already shown that $L^2$ has zero bracket with every $L_i$. Only the linear term contributes: $\begin{aligned}
  \dot L_z&=\{L_z,H\}=0,\\
  \dot L_x&=\{L_x,H\}=c\{L_x,L_z\}=-cL_y,\\
  \dot L_y&=\{L_y,H\}=c\{L_y,L_z\}=cL_x.
  \end{aligned}$

u.src:
The full reduced Hamiltonian is $H=
  \frac{1}{2I}\left(L_x^2+L_y^2+L_z^2\right)+cL_z.$ We have already shown that $L^2$ has zero bracket with every $L_i$. Only the linear term contributes: $\begin{aligned}
  \dot L_z&=\{L_z,H\}=0,\\
  \dot L_x&=\{L_x,H\}=c\{L_x,L_z\}=-cL_y,\\
  \dot L_y&=\{L_y,H\}=c\{L_y,L_z\}=cL_x.
  \end{aligned}$
en:
The full reduced Hamiltonian is $H=
  \frac{1}{2I}\left(L_x^2+L_y^2+L_z^2\right)+cL_z.$ We have already shown that $L^2$ has zero bracket with every $L_i$. Only the linear term contributes: $\begin{aligned}
  \dot L_z&=\{L_z,H\}=0,\\
  \dot L_x&=\{L_x,H\}=c\{L_x,L_z\}=-cL_y,\\
  \dot L_y&=\{L_y,H\}=c\{L_y,L_z\}=cL_x.
  \end{aligned}$

p.src: The final component equations: $L_z$ is constant while $L_x$ and $L_y$ rotate into one another.

p.src:
The vertical component and the horizontal magnitude are constant: $\frac{d}{dt}(L_x^2+L_y^2)
  =2L_x(-cL_y)+2L_y(cL_x)=0.$ Combining the horizontal components, $L_+=L_x+iL_y,
  \qquad
  \dot L_+=icL_+,$ so $L_+(t)=L_+(0)e^{ict}.$ The angular-momentum vector therefore precesses around the vertical axis with angular speed $|c|=MgR/L$. Its tilt remains fixed in this idealized steady motion.
